 Some ballot question brawls may persist past Election Day
 Gintautas Dumcius 
 October 28, 2026 Share Question 1 on the mail-in ballot for the 2026 Massachusetts state election. (Jesse Costa/WBUR) Inside a Malden senior center’s cafeteria earlier this month, about a dozen people settled down at roundtables as their state senator served up a crash course in the record-tying nine ballot questions before voters this year.
 Jason Lewis, who has represented the district covering parts of Middlesex County since 2014, spoke slowly so a young woman standing next to him could translate his explanations into Cantonese.
 “ Ballot initiatives are a wonderful way for regular people — voters — to be able to make your voice heard on a whole range of different issues,” Lewis said.
 From left, Massachusetts Senate President Karen Spilka, state Sen. Jason Lewis, state Rep. Alice Peisch and then-House Speaker Robert DeLeo at a press conference at the Massachusetts State House in Boston in 2019. (Jonathan Wiggs/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) His colleagues in the Legislature — soon-to-be ex-colleagues, as Lewis opted not to run for reelection this year — don’t necessarily agree that they’re the best way to make a law.
 “Having to vote ‘yes’ or ‘no’ on very complicated issues, I think, lends itself to bad policy,” said state Rep. Alice Peisch, a high-ranking leader in the House.
 On Nov. 3, Massachusetts voters have the opportunity to approve or reject nine ballot measures that span topics from a public records law expansion (Question 1) to single-family zoning (Question 7) and a repeal of the state’s marijuana laws (Question 8).
 While the polls will close that night, the fight over the ballot questions may not be over when the results come down. That’s because there’s nothing, beyond the risk of angering the public, that blocks state legislators from tweaking — or even striking — new laws. And on some questions this year, Beacon Hill lawmakers appear poised to have their say.
 The ballot questions in question
 Question 1, in particular, hits close to home for state lawmakers. It would place the Legislature and the governor’s office under the state’s public records law. Massachusetts is the only state where all three branches of government are currently exempt.
 The “yes” side is leading in the polls. But even before voting got underway, lawmakers advanced their own, narrower public records proposal , which would give them more control over the records they’d release to the public.
 Alongside that bill, House lawmakers also proposed blocking state Auditor Diana DiZoglio from taking them to court over her long-sought legislative audit, and limiting her office’s investigatory powers. House and Senate negotiators are working on the final versions of the two proposals.
 DiZoglio is a driving force behind Question 1, mirroring her 2024 ballot question push for the legislative audit. (It was, coincidentally, also named Question 1.)
 Two years ago, 72 percent voted “yes,” but the audit still hasn’t happened amid legal wrangling between the warring camps. House and Senate leaders said it runs afoul of the state Constitution, which calls for the separation of powers between the legislative and executive branch.
 State Auditor Diana DiZoglio speaks to reporters at the State House. (Matt Stone/MediaNews Group/Boston Herald via Getty Images) DiZoglio said their proposal is an effort to “nullify” the legislative audit. She added that lawmakers’ consideration of their own public records law while voting is underway creates, in her words, a “constitutional crisis.”
 Legislators, who are also weighing a response to voters potentially passing Question 5, which would trigger more tax revenue rebates, say they’re acting well within their bounds.
 Asked about DiZoglio’s comments, Peisch, the House lawmaker, called that a “little bit of an extreme description of the current situation,” and said the Legislature can improve voter-approved laws.
 "I don't recall any significant pushback from voters when we did, in fact, amend the details of the legislation."
 state Rep. Alice Peisch She pointed to November 2016, when Massachusetts voted to broadly legalize recreational marijuana, over the deep opposition of Beacon Hill leaders and the popular governor at the time, Charlie Baker.
 The Legislature rewrote the law eight months later, setting up a different regulatory structure, which Baker reluctantly signed . While the voter-approved ballot question regulated marijuana like alcohol, the legislative rewrite gave it similar oversight to what exists over casinos and slots parlors.
 “ The message from the voters was, ‘We want marijuana legalized,’ not necessarily that we want it legalized exactly as the question was written,” Peisch said. “I don't recall any significant pushback from voters when we did, in fact, amend the details of the legislation.”
 Lawmaking power vs. public pressure
 Outright repeals of voter-approved questions are relatively rare. The best known is the Clean Elections law , approved by voters in 1998. It sought to put into place public financing for candidates, but legislators repealed the law in 2003 after a legal battle over funding it.
 For her part, DiZoglio said she doesn’t have a problem with lawmakers making technical fixes. She argued that’s not what’s happened with the legislative audit, or her current push to expand the public records law.
 “ What the Legislature is doing is they are usurping the right of the people of the commonwealth to create laws at the ballot box by, in real-time, simultaneously passing bills to overturn the will of the people,” she said.
 "What the Legislature is doing is they are usurping the right of the people of the commonwealth to create laws at the ballot box ... ."
 State Auditor Diana DiZoglio Rachael Cobb, an associate professor of political science and legal studies at Suffolk University, said legislators have the power to write and rewrite laws, including ones approved by voters.
 “Ultimately, a ballot question is a law, and lawmakers can repeal laws, they can make new laws,” Cobb said. “So there's no granite stone that any of this is written into, and it can change.”
 If people are upset with legislators who rewrite or repeal a ballot law, they do have one powerful option: vote them out.
 “ That's the main way,” Cobb said. “This is the tricky part about being a citizen. You can't always get what you want, and lawmakers can go in a direction that you didn't necessarily exactly want it to go in.”
 But in a state like Massachusetts with few competitive elections, incumbents are rarely tossed out.
 Cobb said citizens can pursue other avenues, but those often require a “high level” of collective action.
 “If they were to form a big enough group and put a lot of pressure on and pull out ads and make life miserable, one could imagine that the Legislature would bend to that before they actually kick them out of office,” she said.
 "Ultimately, a ballot question is a law, and lawmakers can repeal laws, they can make new laws."
 Rachael Cobb Recent polls suggest voters overwhelmingly support the open records law expansion. Still, even if it passes next Tuesday, its fate may not be determined by voters or legislators, but in court.
 DiZoglio told WBUR she’s preparing for another legal battle with the Legislature over Question 1.
 Back in the Malden senior center, Sen. Lewis sought to address the public records ballot question and the Legislature’s competing, narrower proposal.
 “Obviously, you still get to vote on the ballot question,” he said, “but if and when the Legislature does wrap up that work and pass that law, that would supersede the ballot question.”
 He added, in an apologetic tone, “It's a little bit complicated.”
 This segment aired on October 28, 2026. Audio will be available soon.
